questions.question: Explain why a patient with cystic fibrosis and a Mycobacterium infection was given a combination of antibiotics for several months.
questions.answer: Several drugs together make it very unlikely any resistant mutant survives; a long course kills all remaining bacteria.
steps: Bacteria mutate at random, so some cells may already be resistant to one antibiotic.
A single antibiotic would kill sensitive cells and select for resistant mutants, which then multiply (natural selection).
Using a combination makes it very unlikely a bacterium is resistant to all the drugs at once.
Several months of treatment kills all bacteria, including slow-dividing ones that survive short courses.

questions.question: Suggest why the patient, who did not respond to the antibiotics, later needed a lung transplant.
questions.answer: The infection was not cleared, and repeated infection and inflammation destroyed lung tissue so gas exchange failed.
steps: The bacteria were not cleared, so they kept multiplying in the lungs.
Bacterial toxins and the immune response (inflammation) destroy alveolar tissue.
Less alveolar surface area means less oxygen can diffuse into the blood.
Lung function falls too far to survive, so healthy donor lungs are needed.

questions.question: Explain why the Mycobacterium infection developed faster when the patient took drugs that stop DNA synthesis and weaken the immune system.
questions.answer: DNA synthesis is needed for lymphocytes to divide, so fewer T and B cells are made and the immune response is weak.
steps: Drugs block DNA synthesis, so cells cannot copy their DNA before dividing.
B and T lymphocytes cannot divide by mitosis, so clonal expansion is reduced.
Fewer T helper, T killer and plasma cells means less antibody and less killing of infected cells.
With a weak immune response, the bacteria multiply faster and the infection spreads.

questions.question: Explain the changes in the numbers of Mycobacterium and phages after phage therapy started, using the graph.
questions.answer: Phages infect and destroy the bacteria, so bacteria fall after each phage peak, then phages fall as hosts become scarce, giving repeating, falling peaks until both reach zero.
steps: After therapy starts, the number of phages rises as they infect Mycobacterium and replicate inside them, reaching a peak shortly after the first bacterial peak.
When phage numbers are high the bacteria are lysed, so the bacterial number falls from its first peak; the phages then also fall because fewer host bacteria are left for them to reproduce in.

Bacteria that survive (for example because they are not infected) multiply, so a second and a third peak of bacteria occur, each followed by a peak of phages, in a repeating cycle similar to predator and prey; the phage peak always lags the bacterial peak.

The peaks get smaller each time, so the phages (and the patient's immune system) are reducing the infection, and finally the number of bacteria falls to zero, followed by the phages as they have no hosts left.

questions.question: Tick the correct boxes in a table of statements about artificial immunity (artificial active and passive).
questions.answer: Antibodies injected: passive only; B cells differentiate into plasma cells: active only; memory cells are formed: active only.
steps: Injecting antibodies gives artificial passive immunity: the antibodies are ready-made, so the person's own B cells are not involved.
A vaccine (artificial active immunity) stimulates the person's own immune response, so B cells differentiate into plasma cells.
Memory cells are formed only when the person's own lymphocytes respond, so only in active immunity, not passive.

questions.question: Describe the role of macrophages in developing natural active immunity to a virus after infection.
questions.answer: Macrophages engulf the virus, present viral antigens on their surface, and activate T helper cells.
steps: Macrophages engulf viruses by phagocytosis, a non-specific response.
They digest the virus and display viral antigens on their surface bound to MHC class II.
T helper cells with complementary receptors bind to this antigen-MHC complex.
Binding activates the T helper cells, which then trigger B cells and T killer cells to divide.

questions.question: Explain why both T helper cells and T killer cells are needed in the immune response to a virus.
questions.answer: T helper cells activate B cells and T killer cells; T killer cells destroy infected host cells because viruses are inside cells.
steps: Viruses replicate inside host cells, where antibodies cannot reach them.
T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells by clonal selection.
T killer cells bind to and destroy the virus-infected cells, stopping virus replication.
T helper cells also stimulate memory cell formation so the response is faster next time.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term aseptic technique.
questions.answer: Methods used to prevent contamination of cultures by unwanted microorganisms.
steps: Aseptic technique means keeping a culture free from unwanted microorganisms.
It uses sterile equipment and media so only the target species (here E. coli) grows.
This ensures any growth or results come from the organism being studied.
Aseptic technique keeps unwanted microbes out, so only E. coli is being tested.

questions.question: Describe two aseptic techniques that could be used in this investigation.
questions.answer: Flame the neck of bottles and inoculating loops; work near a Bunsen flame and use sterile equipment and media.
steps: Sterilise the inoculating loop or pipette by flaming until red hot before use.
Flame the necks of bottles and tubes when opening and closing them.
Work close to a Bunsen flame so rising hot air keeps airborne microbes away.
Use sterile microdilution plates, tips and media so no unwanted microbes are added.

questions.question: Explain why aseptic technique is important in this investigation.
questions.answer: Contaminating microbes could grow in the wells and make the MIC result inaccurate.
steps: Unwanted microbes could enter the wells from air, skin or equipment.
They could grow and be mistaken for E. coli, showing growth at a concentration where it should not.
This would give a false MIC value for each antimicrobial substance.
Aseptic technique keeps the results valid and reliable.

questions.question: Explain why the microdilution plate was incubated at an appropriate temperature for E. coli for 72 hours.
questions.answer: The temperature matches E. coli's optimum so enzymes work fast, and 72 hours gives enough growth to be visible.
steps: E. coli has an optimum temperature (around 37 C) at which its enzymes work fastest.
At this temperature the bacteria divide quickly and grow in every well with no antimicrobial.
72 hours gives enough cell divisions for visible growth to be seen in the wells.
The MIC is read as the lowest concentration with no visible growth after this time.

questions.question: Explain why an antimicrobial substance that affects E. coli only was included in the assay (row H).
questions.answer: It is a positive control: a substance known to affect E. coli shows that the E. coli can be inhibited and that the method works, and allows the other substances to be compared with it.
steps: The row H substance is known to kill or stop the growth of E. coli, so it acts as a positive control.

If no growth is seen in its low-concentration wells (columns 1 to 5), this shows that the E. coli is sensitive, the method and incubation worked, and any growth in other wells is due to a lack of effect of the substances and not a fault.
It also provides a standard against which the effectiveness of the other seven antimicrobial substances (rows A to G) can be compared.

questions.question: Explain why one column (column 12) had no antimicrobial substance added to it.
questions.answer: It is a negative (growth) control showing the bacteria can grow normally when no antimicrobial is present.
steps: Column 12 has bacteria and medium but no antimicrobial substance.
It shows that the E. coli is viable and grows under the conditions used.
Growth here is compared with the other wells to decide the MIC.
It also shows the medium is not contaminated or sterile so growth cannot be assumed.

questions.question: Describe how a 1 in 2 dilution, to achieve the concentration in this well, would be carried out.
questions.answer: Mix equal volumes of the solution and sterile broth, then spread a sample on agar and count colonies.
steps: Take a known volume of the antimicrobial solution, for example 1 cm3, using a sterile pipette.
Add it to an equal volume (1 cm3) of sterile nutrient broth and mix thoroughly, giving 1 in 2.
Take a sample from this mixture and spread it onto sterile agar.
Incubate and count colonies; the count is halved for each 1 in 2 step.

questions.question: Calculate how many times more effective the antimicrobial in one row is than the antimicrobial in row E, using their MIC columns.
questions.answer: 32 times
steps: Row E: growth starts in column 5, so its MIC is in column 4.
Row G: no growth up to column 9, so its MIC is in column 9.
Each column is a 1 in 2 dilution, so the concentration is halved 5 times from column 4 to column 9: 2^5 = 32.
The substance in row G is effective at 1/32 of the concentration of that in row E, so it is 32 times more effective.

questions.question: Which method is used to find the number of bacteria in this culture (sample added to fresh medium and spread on agar)?
questions.answer: A: dilution plating.
steps: The sample is diluted in fresh medium and spread on agar in a Petri dish.
Each living bacterium that divides forms a colony that can be counted.
This is dilution plating (option A); latency, mass and turbidity methods do not count colonies.
Only dilution plating gives a colony count, so option A is correct.

questions.question: Explain how the Petri dish should have been sealed after the mixture was spread onto the agar.
questions.answer: Seal the lid with tape and incubate the dish upside down, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.
steps: Seal the lid to the base with adhesive tape to stop airborne microbes getting in.
Incubate the dish upside down so condensation forms on the lid, not on the agar.
Droplets falling onto the agar could spread bacteria across it and spoil the count.
Sealing and inverting the dish stops contamination and condensation falling on the agar.

questions.question: Which shows the order of the phases of a bacterial growth curve?
questions.answer: C: lag, exponential, stationary, death.
steps: Bacteria first adapt to the medium in the lag phase.
They divide at a constant rate in the exponential phase.
Growth stops as nutrients run out in the stationary phase, then cells die.
Batch cultures pass through lag, exponential, stationary and death phases in that order.

questions.question: How many of four listed changes (decrease/increase pH, decrease/increase temperature) could result in faster growth?
steps: The bacteria are not at their optimum, so each factor has only one direction of change that would speed growth up.
One of the two pH changes (decrease or increase) would move the pH towards the optimum, and one of the two temperature changes would do the same.
So 2 of the 4 changes would give faster growth.

questions.question: Calculate the growth rate constant (k) of these bacteria between 4 and 10 hours, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: 2.49 (per hour)
steps: From the graph, log10 N at 4 hours = 2.0 (N0) and at 10 hours = 6.5 (Nt), so t = 10 - 4 = 6 hours.
k = 2.49 generations per hour (2 decimal places).

questions.question: Which label should be used for the y-axis of a growth curve from dilution plating (colony counting)?
questions.answer: A: log10 number of living bacterial cells.
steps: Dilution plating counts only living cells that form colonies, so the count is of living cells.
Growth data span a huge range, so a log10 scale is used on the y-axis.
Option A combines both points.
Colony counts give living cells, so option A is chosen over total cell counts.

questions.question: Explain the importance of using an aseptic technique when culturing microorganisms.
questions.answer: It prevents unwanted microorganisms contaminating the culture, which would give false counts or growth.
steps: Unwanted microbes from air, skin or equipment could enter the culture.
They would grow alongside the target microbes and be counted too.
The growth curve or count would then be wrong and not represent the organism studied.
Contamination would give inaccurate counts, so the growth data would not be valid.

questions.question: Explain two aseptic techniques that should be used in dilution plating.
questions.answer: Flame the loop or spreader and work near a Bunsen flame; use sterile pipettes and flame bottle necks.
steps: Flame the spreader or loop until red hot before and after use to kill contaminants.
Work next to a Bunsen flame so rising warm air keeps airborne microbes away.
Use sterile pipettes and diluent so only the target organism is transferred.
Flame the necks of bottles and tubes when opening and closing them.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the increase in cell number between 4 and 6 hours of culture.
questions.answer: About 8.4 x 10^5 (accept about 8.0 to 8.5 x 10^5) cells per cm^3.
steps: Use the calibration graph: number of bacteria is proportional to turbidity, about 1.6 x 10^6 per a.u. (1.45 x 10^6 at 0.9).
Turbidity at 4 h = 0.04 gives about 6.5 x 10^4 cells per cm^3; at 6 h = 0.56 gives about 9.0 x 10^5.

questions.question: Explain the changes in cell number during the first six hours of the culture.
questions.answer: There is no growth for the first 2 hours (lag), a small increase to 4 hours, then very rapid growth between 4 and 6 hours (exponential phase).
steps: 0 to 2 hours: turbidity stays at 0.01 and the increase is 0, because the bacteria are adapting to the medium (lag phase) and making enzymes, so are not yet dividing.
2 to 4 hours: turbidity rises only to 0.04 (an increase of 5.0 x 10^4), because only a few cells have begun to divide.

4 to 6 hours: turbidity rises to 0.56 (an increase of about 8.4 x 10^5), because the bacteria are dividing by binary fission at the maximum rate (exponential phase), with plentiful nutrients, so the cell number rapidly doubles each generation.

questions.question: Describe the method used in dilution plating to count bacterial colonies.
questions.answer: Serially dilute the culture, spread a known volume on agar, incubate, count colonies and multiply by the dilution factor.
steps: Make a series of dilutions of the culture in sterile medium (for example 1 in 10 each time).
Spread a known volume of a suitable dilution onto sterile agar.
Incubate so each living bacterium forms a visible colony.
Count colonies on a plate with 30 to 300 colonies and multiply by the dilution factor.

questions.question: Explain why the numbers of bacteria from turbidity differ from those from dilution plating between 8 and 14 hours.
questions.answer: Turbidity measures all cells, living and dead, while colony counts only include living cells that form colonies.
steps: A photometer measures light absorbed by all cells in the sample, whether alive or dead.
Dilution plating counts only living cells that can divide to form colonies.
As cells die or stop dividing after 8 hours, the colony count falls but turbidity stays high.
So the turbidity method gives a higher number of cells than dilution plating.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the term bactericidal antibiotic.
questions.answer: An antibiotic that kills bacteria.
steps: Bactericidal means bacteria-killing.
The antibiotic causes the death of bacterial cells.
Contrast with bacteriostatic, which only stops them growing or dividing.
Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria, whereas bacteriostatic drugs only inhibit growth.

questions.question: State why antibiotics affect bacteria but usually not the person taking them.
questions.answer: Bacteria have structures (such as a peptidoglycan cell wall and 70S ribosomes) that human cells do not have.
steps: Antibiotics target structures or processes found in prokaryotes but not in human eukaryotic cells.
For example, peptidoglycan cell walls and 70S ribosomes are absent from human cells.
So the drug damages the bacteria without harming the patient's own cells.
This selective toxicity lets antibiotics kill bacteria with little harm to the patient.

questions.question: Describe two pieces of advice given to patients about the use of antibiotics.
questions.answer: Take the full course as prescribed; do not take antibiotics for viral infections or save or share them.
steps: Complete the full course, even if feeling better, so all bacteria are killed.
Do not use antibiotics for viral infections such as colds, which they cannot treat.
Do not save leftover antibiotics or share them, because the wrong dose selects resistant bacteria.
This advice aims to reduce antibiotic resistance and misuse.

questions.question: Describe the effects of this antibiotic on the bacteria present in the throat, using charts before and after treatment.
questions.answer: Types J and K are eliminated by the antibiotic, whereas L, M, N and O survive, so their proportions rise or stay the same (M from about 15% to 26%, N from 22% to 34%).
steps: Before treatment there were six types (J about 17%, K about 6%, L about 26%, M about 15%, N about 22%, O about 13%).
After treatment types J and K are no longer present, so the antibiotic kills these types (they are sensitive to it).

Types L, M, N and O remain, so are not affected (resistant); their proportion increases, with M from about 15% to 26% and N from about 22% to 34%, while L (about 27%) and O (about 12%) are about the same, and the charts show proportions, not the total numbers.

questions.question: Compare and contrast bacteriostatic antibiotics with bactericidal antibiotics.
questions.answer: Both stop bacterial growth; bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, while bacteriostatic ones only stop them growing and dividing.
steps: Both types inhibit bacterial growth or reproduction, so both act on bacteria.
Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop growth and division, so the bacteria remain alive.
Bactericidal antibiotics kill the bacteria outright.
Bacteriostatic bacteria can recover once the drug is removed if the immune system does not clear them.

questions.question: Describe how the chromatogram of one antibiotic could be produced.
questions.answer: Spot the sample on a baseline, stand paper in a solvent so it rises by capillary action, then locate spots and measure distances to calculate Rf.
steps: Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom of chromatography paper and spot the antibiotic sample on it.
Place the paper in a solvent below the baseline so the solvent does not dissolve the spot.
As the solvent moves up by capillary action, the antibiotic separates according to solubility and attraction to the paper.
Locate the spots (for example under UV), then Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front.

questions.question: Which option identifies the antibiotic in the diagram and the method used?
questions.answer: B: tetracycline using method 2.
steps: Rf = distance moved by the spot from the origin / distance moved by the solvent front from the origin.
On the chromatogram the spot is about 151 mm from the origin and the solvent front is about 205 mm from the origin.
Rf = 151 / 205 = 0.74, which is closest to 0.75, the Rf of tetracycline using method 2.

questions.question: Explain why the four Rf values in the table are all different from each other.
questions.answer: Each antibiotic has different solubility and affinity for the solvent and paper, and the two methods use different conditions.
steps: Each antibiotic has its own solubility in the solvent and attraction to the stationary phase.
So each travels a different distance relative to the solvent front.
The two methods use different solvents or stationary phases, which change the distances moved.
So the four Rf values differ for the two antibiotics and two methods.

questions.question: Suggest the difference between active and passive immunotherapy.
questions.answer: Active immunotherapy stimulates the patient's own immune system to respond; passive immunotherapy gives ready-made antibodies or immune cells.
steps: Active immunotherapy stimulates the patient's own immune system to make antibodies and immune cells.
This produces an immune response and memory cells in the patient.
Passive immunotherapy gives the patient ready-made antibodies or activated immune cells.
No immune response is needed from the patient, so the effect is immediate but short-lived.

questions.question: Explain how a mutation can result in the formation of a neoantigen.
questions.answer: A mutation changes the base sequence of a gene, altering the amino acid sequence and shape of the membrane protein so it is seen as foreign.
steps: A mutation changes a base in DNA, which changes a codon in the mRNA.
The changed codon codes for a different amino acid, or none, in the protein.
The altered amino acid sequence changes the protein's tertiary structure and shape.
The new shape is not present on normal cells, so it acts as a neoantigen recognised by the immune system.

questions.question: Explain how vaccines containing mRNA coding for neoantigens stimulate the immune response.
questions.answer: The mRNA is translated into neoantigen, which is presented on MHC to T cells, causing clonal expansion of T cells that kill cancer cells.
steps: The mRNA enters cells, such as antigen-presenting cells, and ribosomes translate it into the neoantigen protein.
The neoantigen is processed and presented on MHC molecules on the cell surface.
T helper and T killer cells with matching receptors bind to the complex and are activated, then divide by clonal expansion.
T killer cells destroy cancer cells displaying the neoantigen, and memory cells remain for future protection.

questions.question: Explain how monoclonal antibodies (identical antibodies specific to one antigen) help the immune system destroy cancer cells.
questions.answer: They bind specifically to the cancer antigen, marking the cancer cells for destruction by phagocytes or other immune cells.
steps: Each monoclonal antibody has a binding site complementary to one specific cancer antigen.
It binds to antigens on the cancer cells, so it targets only those cells.
Bound antibodies mark the cancer cells so phagocytes such as macrophages engulf them (opsonisation).
Antibodies can also activate complement or block receptors that help cancer cells grow.

questions.question: Explain why large numbers of genetically identical T cells must be made for adoptive cell therapy to be effective.
questions.answer: All identical cells carry the same receptor for the cancer antigen, and large numbers are needed to kill enough cancer cells.
steps: Genetically identical cells all have the same receptor specific to one cancer antigen.
Large numbers ensure enough cells are present to bind and kill the many cancer cells.
Cloning in the laboratory produces the required numbers from the patient's own T cells.
Enough cells are needed to overcome the tumour and provide a lasting response.

questions.question: Suggest two features of a virus that make it suitable for oncolytic virotherapy.
questions.answer: It infects and replicates in cancer cells selectively, and it is non-pathogenic (harmless) to normal human cells.
steps: The virus should infect and replicate mainly in cancer cells, not in healthy cells.
It should lyse (burst) the cancer cells through the lytic cycle, releasing new viruses to spread.
It should be non-pathogenic, so it does not cause disease in the patient.
Such a virus needs receptors on cancer cells to attach to them.

questions.question: Which type of glycosidic bond is broken in the digestion of cellulose? (options A to D)
questions.answer: A: beta 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
steps: Cellulose is a polymer of glucose linked by beta 1-4 glycosidic bonds.
Cellulase enzymes break these beta 1-4 bonds to release glucose.
Option A is the only option with beta 1-4; the symbol in the text is garbled, but 1-4 matches cellulose.
Digestion by hydrolysis adds water to break these bonds and release glucose.

questions.question: Put one cross in each row to show whether genes are found in each structure of bacteria and fungi.
questions.answer: Mitochondria: fungi only; nuclei: fungi only; 70S ribosomes: neither (they contain rRNA and protein, not genes).
steps: Mitochondria contain their own DNA (genes) and are found only in eukaryotes, so only in the fungi: fungi only.
The nucleus contains the chromosomes (genes) and is found only in eukaryotes, so only in the fungi: fungi only.

70S ribosomes are made of rRNA and protein and do not contain genes (the genes for rRNA are in the DNA), so as written the answer is neither; if the question meant which organisms have 70S ribosomes, it would be both, because bacteria have 70S ribosomes and fungal mitochondria also have them.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the succession of bacteria during development of a giant panda (options A to D)?
questions.answer: C: Escherichia and Shigella, then Streptococcus, then Clostridium (the order in which each group peaks, from cubs to adults).
steps: The graph has three groups of bars: one highest in cubs and falling with age, one highest in young animals, and one rising to be highest in adults, which gives the order of succession.
Escherichia and Shigella are early colonisers of the gut and are most abundant in cubs.

Clostridium (anaerobic bacteria that digest cellulose) increases as the panda starts eating bamboo, so is most abundant in adults, with Streptococcus in between; the group names are not shown on the page, so this order is based on this biology, giving option C.

questions.question: Describe one method that could be used to determine the relative abundance of Streptococcus in a giant panda's intestines.
questions.answer: Extract DNA from faecal samples, amplify a 16S rRNA gene by PCR, sequence it, and count reads matching Streptococcus.
steps: Collect faecal samples from the panda and extract the total DNA from the bacteria.
Use PCR with primers for the 16S rRNA gene, which is present in all bacteria but varies between species.
Sequence the amplified DNA and match the sequences to a database to identify Streptococcus.
Relative abundance = number of Streptococcus sequences / total bacterial sequences x 100%.

questions.question: Describe the information that had to be collected by scientists before drug ATD could be approved for Alzheimer's disease.
questions.answer: Evidence of effectiveness (compared with a placebo) and safety, including side effects, from clinical trials.
steps: Trials show whether the drug reduces Alzheimer's symptoms or plaques compared with a placebo group.
A control group receives a placebo so the effect of the drug is separated from other factors.
Side effects and safety at different doses are recorded to ensure the drug is not harmful.
Data must be reproducible across many patients before approval.

questions.question: Explain the phrase 'an antibody that is specific for beta-amyloid'.
questions.answer: The antibody's binding site is complementary in shape to one antigen (beta-amyloid) and binds only to it.
steps: Each antibody has a variable region whose binding site has a specific shape.
This binding site is complementary to a particular antigen, here beta-amyloid.
Only beta-amyloid with this shape fits and binds, so other antigens are not bound.
Specificity comes from the shape of the variable region, so only beta-amyloid binds.

questions.question: Suggest how drug ATD could reduce the build-up of beta-amyloid in the brains of people with Alzheimer's.
questions.answer: The antibody binds to beta-amyloid, marking it for removal by phagocytes, and stops further aggregation into plaques.
steps: The antibody binds to the beta-amyloid protein by forming an antigen-antibody complex.
Bound antibodies mark the amyloid so that phagocytes such as macrophages engulf and remove it.
Binding also blocks beta-amyloid from clumping into plaques.
So less beta-amyloid builds up in the brain.

questions.question: Suggest why the elderly person, from whom the B memory cell for drug ATD was taken, did not have Alzheimer's disease.
questions.answer: Their immune system probably made antibodies that bound beta-amyloid and prevented plaques from building up.
steps: Their B cells produced antibodies that bind to beta-amyloid and clear it.
Without build-up of plaques, the neurones were not damaged.
So they showed no signs of Alzheimer's disease.
Early clearance of beta-amyloid would prevent plaques from forming.

questions.question: Explain why this drug could be produced only from B memory cells taken from a person who did not have Alzheimer's disease.
questions.answer: A person with Alzheimer's disease has not made effective antibodies against beta-amyloid, so only a person without the disease has B memory cells with the gene for an antibody that clears beta-amyloid.
steps: The drug is an antibody specific to beta-amyloid, so the B memory cells used must make an effective antibody for it.
In a person with Alzheimer's disease the beta-amyloid has built up into plaques, showing that their immune system has not made antibodies that destroy it.
B memory cells from a person without the disease make antibodies that remove beta-amyloid and prevent plaques, so these cells provide the gene for the effective antibody.

questions.question: Which viruses contain the same type of nucleic acid as Ebola virus (RNA)?
questions.answer: B: HIV and tobacco mosaic virus (TMV).
steps: Ebola virus has RNA as its genetic material.
HIV and TMV are both RNA viruses.
Lambda phage has DNA, so option B is correct.
Matching the nucleic acid type gives option B.

questions.question: Which viruses have a helical capsid?
questions.answer: D: tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) only.
steps: TMV has a helical capsid of protein subunits wound around its RNA.
HIV has a different (conical) capsid, not helical.
Lambda phage has a complex capsid, so option D is correct.
Option D is the only virus in the list with a helical capsid.

questions.question: What type of molecule makes up the capsid of a virus?
questions.answer: D: protein.
steps: The capsid is the protein coat that surrounds the viral nucleic acid.
Capsids are made of protein subunits (capsomeres).
Protein subunits make up the capsid, so option D is correct.
Capsid proteins protect the viral nucleic acid from damage.

questions.question: Calculate how many times larger the Ebola virus (volume 7.76 x 10^4 nm3) is than TMV (300 nm long, 80 nm diameter, cylinder).
questions.answer: About 0.05 times, so Ebola is about 19 times smaller than TMV.
steps: TMV radius = 80 / 2 = 40 nm; length = 300 nm.
Volume of TMV = pi x 40^2 x 300 = about 1.51 x 10^6 nm3.
Ratio = Ebola volume / TMV volume = 7.76 x 10^4 / 1.51 x 10^6 = about 0.051.
So Ebola is about 0.05 times the size of TMV (TMV is about 19 times larger).

questions.question: Name the two enzymes found in HIV that are not found in most other viruses.
questions.answer: Reverse transcriptase and integrase.
steps: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the viral RNA template.
Integrase inserts the viral DNA into the host cell genome.
Both enzymes are carried into the host cell inside the virus particle.
Reverse transcriptase and integrase are both needed for HIV to integrate.

questions.question: Explain why HIV contains these two enzymes.
questions.answer: Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA, and integrase inserts that DNA into the host genome so it can be replicated.
steps: HIV's genetic material is RNA, but host cells copy DNA, so reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA from the RNA.
Integrase then joins the viral DNA into the host cell's chromosomal DNA as a provirus.
The integrated viral DNA is transcribed and translated by the host cell to make new viral RNA and proteins.
So the virus is copied each time the host cell divides.

questions.question: Which option describes an enzyme in a living organism?
questions.answer: C: an organic substance that decreases activation energy.
steps: Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein, which is organic.
Enzymes work by lowering the activation energy of a reaction.
Options A and B are inorganic, and D describes the wrong effect on activation energy.
Option C is correct: an organic (protein) catalyst that decreases activation energy.

questions.question: Name the type of scale used on the y-axis of the survival time graph for fish.
questions.answer: A logarithmic scale (log10).
steps: The y-axis values 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 are equal distances apart, so each step is a 10-fold increase.
This is a logarithmic (log10) scale, not a linear one.

questions.question: Which two biotic factors could cause fish to die within the zone of tolerance (options A to D)?
questions.answer: C: predators and pathogens.
steps: Biotic factors are living things, such as predators and pathogens.
Pathogens cause disease and predators kill fish in the zone of tolerance.
Salt level and wave action are abiotic (non-living) factors, so A, B and D are wrong.
Option C is the only pair of living (biotic) factors.

questions.question: Explain why the survival time of fish is reduced at temperatures lower and higher than those in the zone of tolerance.
questions.answer: At high temperatures enzymes denature and at low temperatures reactions slow, so the fish cannot maintain metabolism and survive.
steps: Fish body temperature follows the water temperature because they are ectotherms.
At high temperatures, enzymes denature because hydrogen bonds break and the active site changes shape.
At low temperatures, kinetic energy falls, so enzyme-controlled reactions such as respiration slow down.
Either way, the fish cannot maintain its metabolism, so its survival time is reduced.

questions.question: Calculate the Q10 for this enzyme stored for 3 hours, using the formula and initial rate at 20 C.
steps: Read the graph for the enzyme stored for 3 hours: the rate at 20 C (R_t) = 2.7 a.u.
The rate at 30 C (R_t+10) = 4.3 a.u.

questions.question: Explain why the optimum temperature for this enzyme is affected by storage time.
questions.answer: With longer storage some enzyme molecules denature, so the rate falls and the optimum shifts to a lower temperature (about 45 C after 3 h, about 38 C after 10 h, about 33 C after 26 h).
steps: During storage the enzyme molecules gradually lose their tertiary structure (bonds such as hydrogen bonds break), so the active site changes shape and fewer enzyme molecules can bind substrate, giving a lower maximum rate.
The enzyme molecules that are left are partly unfolded and less stable, so they are denatured by heat at a lower temperature than fresh enzyme.
So the optimum temperature falls as storage time increases (from about 41 to 49 C for 3 hours to about 38 C for 10 hours and about 33 C for 26 hours).

questions.question: Explain why forensic entomology is the most accurate method for estimating time of death when this is greater than 72 hours.
questions.answer: After 72 hours other methods are unreliable, but insect succession follows predictable life cycles that show how long insects have been feeding.
steps: Body temperature and other physical signs stop changing reliably after about 72 hours.
Insects colonise a body in a predictable sequence called succession.
The stage of development of the insect larvae can be aged, giving the time since colonisation.
This gives a more accurate time of death than other methods after 72 hours.

questions.question: Explain how forensic entomology can indicate whether a body has been moved from the place of death.
questions.answer: Insect species found on the body that do not live in the local area show the body was moved from another habitat.
steps: Each insect species is adapted to a particular habitat and climate.
If species found on the body are not those expected at the place of death, the body was probably moved.
Insects found on the body may also differ in development stage from those on the ground nearby.
This indicates that insect colonisation happened somewhere else.

questions.question: Suggest why the mammal was placed inside a metal cage to decompose.
questions.answer: To keep out scavenging animals so that only insects and microbes decompose the body.
steps: Larger scavengers such as birds and mammals would remove or scatter the body.
The cage keeps the body in place so decomposition by insects and microbes can be monitored.
This makes the results valid and reproducible.
The cage keeps the carcass intact so decomposition can be monitored.

questions.question: Calculate the rate of change in mass between day 5 and day 15 of decomposition, in kg per hour to two decimal places.
questions.answer: 0.08 kg per hour (a decrease in mass).
steps: From the graph, the mass at day 5 is 22 kg and at day 15 it is 3 kg.
Change in mass = 3 - 22 = -19 kg over 10 days, which is 10 x 24 = 240 hours.
Rate = 19 / 240 = 0.079 = 0.08 kg per hour (loss).

questions.question: Explain the changes in mass of the mammal during decomposition.
questions.answer: Mass is almost constant when fresh, falls fastest during the active stage when maggots and microorganisms break down soft tissue, then falls slowly to about 1 kg of remains (hair, bone and dry skin).
steps: Fresh and bloated stages (0 to 5 days): mass falls only slightly (from 23 to 22 kg) because the body is still intact, with only a small loss of fluid and gas from bacterial action.

Active stage (5 to 10 days): mass falls rapidly (from 22 to about 9 kg) as the body ruptures, fly larvae (maggots) feed on the soft tissue, and bacteria and fungi decompose proteins and fats; liquids drain away and gases are lost.
Advanced stage (10 to 15 days): mass falls more slowly (to about 3 kg) as little soft tissue is left to feed on.
Remains stage: mass becomes steady at about 1 kg because only tough materials such as bone, hair and dry skin remain, which decompose very slowly.

questions.question: Suggest why some insect eggs collected from the decomposing mammal were taken to the laboratory and kept for a few days.
questions.answer: To let the eggs hatch and develop so the insect species can be identified and aged.
steps: Eggs take time to hatch into larvae that are easier to identify than eggs.
Identifying the species allows the development time to be looked up for estimating time of death.
Keeping them at controlled temperatures lets development be monitored accurately.
Keeping the eggs lets the larvae develop so their age and species can be determined.

questions.question: Explain how the data in the table illustrate succession.
questions.answer: Different insect species dominate at different stages: Lucilia first (100% when fresh), then Cochliomyia (68.4% in the active stage), then Ophyra (30.9% advanced and 83.9% in the remains).
steps: Lucilia are the first colonisers: 100% of insects when fresh and 61.4% when bloated, but only 1.8% in the active stage.
Cochliomyia replaces them, peaking at 68.4% in the active stage and then falling to 35.1% (advanced) and 0% (remains).
Ophyra appears later (0.6% active, 30.9% advanced) and dominates the remains (83.9%), and Fannia only appears in the advanced stage (0.1%).
Each species is replaced as the body changes (conditions change from fresh tissue to dry remains), which is succession.

questions.question: Which labelled structure of the HIV diagram is RNA (options A to D: R, Q, S, T)?
questions.answer: B: Q
steps: The RNA is the genetic material inside the capsid; it is the long thread-like strand in the centre of the virus.
R, S and T are the glycoprotein, matrix and capsid, which are made of protein, so only Q is RNA.

questions.question: How many of structures Q, R and S of the HIV diagram contain protein (options A to D)?
steps: R is a glycoprotein spike in the envelope, so it contains protein.
S is the matrix or capsid layer, which is made of protein.
Q is the RNA, which is not protein, so only R and S (2 structures) contain protein.

questions.question: Which virus has structure P and contains RNA (options A to D)?
questions.answer: A: Ebola virus only.
steps: P is the lipid envelope that surrounds the capsid in HIV.
Ebola virus has a lipid envelope and RNA, so it has structure P.
Tobacco mosaic virus has only a helical capsid and RNA, and has no envelope.

questions.question: The diameter of HIV is 120 nm. Which is the approximate magnification of the drawing (options A to D)?
steps: Magnification = image size / actual size.
The diameter of the drawing (envelope) is about 5.4 cm on the page, which is 5.4 x 10^7 nm.
Magnification = 5.4 x 10^7 / 120 = 4.5 x 10^5, about x 500 000.

questions.question: Explain why the number of people infected with HIV was divided by 10 on the graph.
questions.answer: The infection numbers are much larger than deaths, so dividing by 10 brings both data sets onto a readable common scale.
steps: The number of people infected is far larger than the number of deaths.
Plotting both on the same axis would make the deaths line almost flat at the bottom.
Dividing by 10 keeps both sets of values on a similar scale so trends can be compared.
The scaling must be stated on the graph so the true numbers can be read.

questions.question: Calculate the mean rate of increase in the number of people infected with HIV from 2005 to 2010, in standard form.
questions.answer: About 2 x 10^5 people per year (accept about 2 to 3 x 10^5).
steps: Read the graph: the number of people infected is about 3.1 (x10 = 31 million) in 2005 and about 3.2 (x10 = 32 million) in 2010; the graph values are divided by 10.
Increase = 32 million - 31 million = 1 x 10^6 over 5 years.
Mean rate = 1 x 10^6 / 5 = 2 x 10^5 people per year (reading to 3.07 and 3.20 gives 2.6 x 10^5).

questions.question: Explain why the number of people infected with HIV is going up after 2005 although new infections and deaths are going down.
questions.answer: New infections still exceed deaths, so the total number of people living with HIV rises.
steps: The number of people living with HIV = previous total + new infections - deaths.
New infections are still greater than deaths after 2005, even though both are falling.
So the total living with HIV keeps increasing.
People on treatment also survive longer, so they remain in the infected total.

questions.question: State how the graph can be used to estimate the number of deaths in 2025.
questions.answer: Extend the trend line (extrapolate) beyond 2017 and read off the number of deaths at 2025.
steps: Draw or extend the line of best fit of deaths against year beyond 2017.
Find the point on the extended line corresponding to 2025.
Read the number of deaths from the y-axis at that point.
Extrapolation assumes the trend continues, so the estimate is approximate.

questions.question: Explain why the estimate of deaths in 2025 would be lower if a vaccine for HIV became available in 2023.
questions.answer: A vaccine gives immunity, so fewer people become infected, which means fewer deaths from HIV later.
steps: A vaccine stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells against HIV.
People vaccinated are protected, so fewer people become newly infected from 2023.
Fewer infections mean fewer people reach the stage of AIDS and die of the disease.
So the number of deaths in 2025 would be lower than the trend-line estimate.

questions.question: Which row of the table shows the cells that present antigens to T helper and T killer cells?
questions.answer: C: macrophages present antigens to T helper cells, and host-infected cells present antigens to T killer cells.
steps: Macrophages engulf pathogens and present the antigens on their surface to T helper cells.
T killer cells recognise antigens displayed on the surface of host cells that are infected (or cancerous), which they then destroy.
Only row C has macrophages for T helper cells and host-infected cells for T killer cells.

questions.question: Which virus would be suitable for Step 2 (inserting the CAR gene) if it is modified to be non-pathogenic (options A to D)?
questions.answer: B: human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which is a retrovirus that can insert genes into host cell DNA.
steps: Step 2 inserts the CAR gene into T cells, so a vector that can deliver genetic material is needed.
HIV is a retrovirus that inserts its genetic material into host cell DNA, so it can be used as a vector.
Ebola, lambda phage and TMV are not suitable: Ebola is highly pathogenic, while lambda phage infects bacteria and TMV infects plants.
Only HIV, modified to be non-pathogenic, can insert genes, so option B is correct.

questions.question: Explain why the CAR gene is inserted into the T cells in Step 3.
questions.answer: So the T cells make the CAR receptor on their surface, which binds the specific cancer antigen and allows them to kill cancer cells.
steps: The CAR gene codes for a receptor that binds a specific antigen on the cancer cells.
Inserting the gene makes the T cells produce this CAR receptor on their membrane.
CAR-T cells can then bind to the cancer antigen and destroy the cancer cells.
Without the CAR gene the T cells cannot make the receptor needed to bind cancer cells.

questions.question: Explain the importance of mitosis in the replication of the CAR-T cells in Step 4.
questions.answer: Mitosis makes genetically identical daughter cells, each carrying the CAR gene, so large numbers of cancer-specific T cells are produced.
steps: Mitosis produces daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent CAR-T cell.
Each daughter cell carries the inserted CAR gene and makes the same CAR receptor.
This clonal expansion produces large numbers of cells with the same specificity for the cancer antigen.
Enough cells are needed to kill the cancer cells in the patient's body.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of injecting CAR-T cells into the same patient they were taken from (Step 5).
questions.answer: The cells are the patient's own, so they are not rejected, and no immunosuppressive drugs are needed.
steps: Cells from the same patient have the patient's own MHC and antigens, so they are recognised as self.
This avoids an immune rejection response against the injected cells.
No immunosuppressive drugs are needed, so the patient's immune system stays active.
The cells can persist in the body and act as memory cells for future protection.

questions.question: Suggest why CAR-T cells are not effective against cancer cells in solid tumours growing in other tissues.
questions.answer: CAR-T cells cannot easily reach or penetrate the solid tumour, and solid tumours often have fewer suitable antigens.
steps: T cells in the blood must reach the tumour, which is hard to penetrate in solid tissue.
Solid tumours create a suppressive environment that inhibits T cell activity.
Solid tumour cells may lack a single uniform antigen target that the CAR receptor binds.
Solid tumours need immune cells to penetrate tissue, which limits CAR-T cells.

questions.question: Explain why HIV is an immunodeficiency virus.
questions.answer: HIV infects and destroys T helper cells, so fewer T helper cells are available to activate B and T killer cells, weakening immunity.
steps: HIV binds to CD4 receptors on T helper cells and enters them.
It replicates inside the T helper cells and causes them to be destroyed.
With fewer T helper cells, B cells and T killer cells are not activated, so fewer antibodies are made.
The body cannot fight off infections, so opportunistic infections and disease result.

questions.question: Explain how reverse transcriptase inhibitors and integrase inhibitors reduce the development of HIV.
questions.answer: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors stop viral RNA being copied to DNA; integrase inhibitors stop the viral DNA being inserted into the host genome.
steps: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors block the enzyme that makes DNA from HIV's RNA.
Without viral DNA, the virus cannot integrate into the host cell genome.
Integrase inhibitors block the enzyme that inserts viral DNA into the host chromosome.
So new viral proteins and particles are not made, so HIV replication is reduced.

questions.question: Suggest why patients are given combinations of antiretroviral drugs.
questions.answer: HIV mutates rapidly, so combining drugs makes it unlikely that a resistant strain will survive all of them.
steps: HIV mutates quickly, so some viruses may be resistant to one drug.
A single drug would select for these resistant strains, which would then multiply.
Using several drugs together makes it very unlikely a virus is resistant to all of them.
This keeps the viral load low for longer.

questions.question: Suggest why the number of HIV virus particles increases if a patient stops taking antiretroviral drugs.
questions.answer: Some HIV DNA is integrated into host cells as a provirus and survives; when the drugs stop, it is activated and replicates again.
steps: Antiretroviral drugs stop replication but do not remove HIV DNA already in host cells.
Some infected cells hold HIV as integrated provirus that is latent and not killed.
When drugs stop, the provirus is activated and produces new virus particles.
So the viral population rises again.

questions.question: Explain the importance of antibodies in the immune response.
questions.answer: Antibodies bind specific antigens, causing agglutination, neutralising toxins and viruses, and marking pathogens for phagocytosis.
steps: Each antibody binds to a specific antigen on a pathogen, due to its complementary binding site.
Binding can clump pathogens together (agglutination) so they are easier to engulf.
Antibodies neutralise toxins and block viruses from attaching to host cells.
Antibodies mark pathogens for phagocytosis by macrophages and activate complement.

questions.question: Describe the changes in classes of antibody in a fetus before birth and in a child after birth, using the graph.
questions.answer: Maternal IgG appears about 6 months before birth, rises to about 1100 mg per 100 cm^3 at birth, then falls to near zero by about 10 months, while the child's own IgG starts at birth and rises to about 600 by 12 months, and IgA stays very low.
steps: Before birth: IgG from the mother first appears at about 6 months before birth and rises steeply to a peak of about 1100 mg per 100 cm^3 at birth (it crosses the placenta).
After birth: IgG from the mother falls rapidly to about 200 at 2 months, about 50 at 4 months and about 0 by 9 to 10 months, because it is broken down and not replaced.
The child makes its own IgG from birth, rising slowly then to about 200 at 2 months, 350 at 4 months and about 600 at 12 months.
IgA from the mother is at a very low concentration, rising only slightly after birth to about 80 at 12 months.

questions.question: Which type of immunity explains the presence of IgA in a baby (options A to D)?
questions.answer: D: natural passive immunity.
steps: IgA is transferred to the baby in breast milk (colostrum), not made by the baby.
This is natural, because it happens through breastfeeding.
Antibodies that are passed from another person are passive immunity, so the answer is D.
IgA from breast milk is passive and natural, so the answer is option D.

questions.question: Suggest why antibody concentration is less in a child 12 months after birth than in an adult.
questions.answer: The child's immune system is still developing and has been exposed to fewer pathogens, so fewer antibodies and memory cells have been produced.
steps: A child's immune system is still developing and has had less exposure to pathogens.
Fewer B cells have been activated, so fewer antibodies are produced.
Maternal antibodies received at birth have declined over time.
Adults have built up memory cells from many infections, so higher antibody levels.

questions.question: Give one piece of evidence, shown in the photographs, that rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory condition.
questions.answer: Swelling of the joints (knuckles and fingers) in the hand with rheumatoid arthritis compared with the normal hand.
steps: The photograph of the affected hand shows swollen, enlarged finger joints (knuckles) that make the hand and fingers look distorted.
Swelling is a sign of inflammation, and it is not present in the normal hand.

questions.question: Give two other signs of inflammation experienced in the hand of a person with rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.answer: Heat and pain.
steps: Inflammation is characterised by redness, heat, swelling and pain.
The redness and swelling are visible in the photograph, so the other two signs are heat and pain.
Heat results from increased blood flow, and pain from chemicals stimulating nerve endings.
Redness, swelling, heat and pain are the four signs of inflammation.

questions.question: Explain how attaching the TNF gene to the viral gene results in TNF being displayed on the outside of the capsid.
questions.answer: The TNF gene is joined to the gene for a capsid or surface protein, so a fusion protein is made that carries TNF out to the outside of the virus.
steps: The TNF gene is inserted next to the viral capsid protein gene in the same DNA or RNA.
Both are transcribed and translated together to make a single fusion protein.
The viral part of the fusion protein is incorporated into the capsid, carrying TNF to its outer surface.
So TNF is displayed on the outside of the capsid where it can be detected and used to make antibodies.

questions.question: Explain why antibodies to TNF are used to treat rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.answer: TNF causes inflammation; antibodies bind to TNF and block its receptors, so inflammation and damage to joints is reduced.
steps: TNF binds receptors on cell membranes and causes inflammation in the joints.
Anti-TNF antibodies bind to TNF, preventing it from binding its receptors.
With TNF blocked, the chemical reactions causing inflammation are reduced.
So the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis are relieved.

questions.question: Explain why patients being treated with antibodies to TNF can die from tuberculosis.
questions.answer: TNF stimulates macrophages to contain and destroy TB bacteria, so blocking TNF lets TB spread and become fatal.
steps: TNF stimulates macrophages and other immune cells to activate phagocytosis of bacteria.
TNF helps form granulomas that wall off Mycobacterium tuberculosis and stop it spreading.
When TNF is blocked, macrophages are less active and granulomas do not form properly.
The TB bacteria multiply and spread through the lungs and body, which can be fatal.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the four characteristics of inflammation.
questions.answer: Redness, heat, swelling and pain.
steps: Inflammation has four characteristics: redness, heat, swelling and pain.
Redness and heat come from increased blood flow to the area.
Swelling is caused by fluid leaking from capillaries into the tissue.
Pain is caused by chemicals stimulating nerve endings.

questions.question: Describe the role of two characteristics of inflammation in response to a cut to the skin.
questions.answer: Heat and redness show increased blood flow that brings phagocytes and clotting factors; swelling and pain protect and immobilise the area.
steps: Increased blood flow (redness and heat) brings phagocytes and nutrients to the wound.
Heat also increases enzyme activity of white blood cells and inhibits pathogen growth.
Swelling caused by leaking fluid dilutes toxins and allows antibodies and clotting factors to reach the area.
Pain makes the person protect the wound, reducing further damage.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the effect of treating inflammation with curcumin extract and drug A, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both treatments reduce inflammation below the untreated level and both reduce it more over the 6 days, but curcumin extract is more effective than drug A on every day, especially on days 1 and 2.
steps: Similarity: with both curcumin extract and drug A inflammation is below the level with no treatment (the dashed line), and it generally falls as the days go by (day 6 lowest for both).
Difference: curcumin extract gives lower inflammation than drug A on all six days, e.g. on day 1 it is about half of drug A, and on day 2 about 40%.

Difference: with drug A inflammation is highest on day 2 and then falls, whereas curcumin has a smaller fall over the first 3 days and then falls to its lowest level at day 6; the gap between them is greatest on day 2 and smaller by day 6.

questions.question: A sample of turmeric contains 3% curcumin. Which is the mass of turmeric needed for one 1 g curcumin treatment (options A to D)?
steps: Mass of curcumin needed = 1 g.
Mass of turmeric = mass of curcumin / percentage = 1 / 0.03.
1 / 0.03 = 33.3 g, which is option C.
Option C is correct: 1 / 0.03 = 33.3 g.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term infection.
questions.answer: The invasion and multiplication of a pathogen in the host's body, which causes disease.
steps: Infection means a pathogen enters the host and multiplies inside it.
The pathogen causes damage and disease symptoms.
Infection differs from disease, which is the harm that results.
Infection describes the pathogen living and multiplying inside the host.

questions.question: Which is the approximate death rate from malaria in 2019, given 229 million cases and 4.09 x 10^5 deaths (options A to D)?
steps: Divide the number of cases by the number of deaths: 229 000 000 / 409 000 = about 560.
560 is closest to 1 in 600 among the options.
So the death rate is about 1 in 600, option B.
Option B (1 in 600) is the closest value.

questions.question: In 2019, 274 000 young children died from malaria out of 409 000 total deaths. Which is the ratio of deaths in young children to other age groups (options A to D)?
steps: Deaths in other age groups = 409 000 - 274 000 = 135 000.
This is closest to 2.0 : 1.0, option D.
Option D (2.0 : 1.0) is the closest ratio.

questions.question: Suggest why living sporozoites are used in a vaccine against malaria.
questions.answer: Sporozoites present the malaria antigens to the immune system, so memory cells are produced, and the living form gives a strong, long-lasting response.
steps: Sporozoites carry the antigens of Plasmodium that the immune system needs to recognise.
Living (weakened) parasites are better at stimulating an immune response than dead ones.
The immune system produces antibodies and T cells and memory cells against the sporozoite antigens.
Memory cells give a fast response if the person is later infected with the real malaria parasite.

questions.question: Deduce why two chemicals were injected with the vaccine in clinical trials, one killing sporozoites and the other killing merozoites.
questions.answer: To kill the living vaccine sporozoites before they reach the liver and stop them causing malaria, and to kill merozoites so they cannot infect red blood cells.
steps: The vaccine contains living sporozoites, which could cause malaria if they reached the liver.
One chemical kills the sporozoites so they cannot infect liver cells and cause disease.
The other chemical kills any merozoites that form, so they cannot invade red blood cells.
Together they make the vaccine safe to test, while the immune response to the antigens is still stimulated.

questions.question: Explain why the vaccine was effective against both strains of sporozoites when people were infected three months after vaccination.
questions.answer: Memory cells persist from the vaccination and respond quickly, and the two strains share some antigens that the immune system recognises.
steps: Memory B and T cells made after vaccination are still present three months later.
These memory cells respond rapidly on re-exposure, giving a secondary immune response.
The identical strain carries the same antigens, so it is recognised directly.
The different strain shares some antigens with the vaccine strain, so the same memory cells also recognise it.

questions.question: Explain the use of antibiotics to treat the medical conditions shown in the table.
questions.answer: Antibiotics kill or stop the growth of bacteria, so they are needed for the bacterial infections (impetigo, whooping cough) and only sometimes for ear and sinus infections, which can be caused by bacteria or viruses, and not for multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis, which are not infections.
steps: Impetigo and whooping cough are caused by bacteria, so antibiotics are needed.
Middle ear and sinus infections are sometimes caused by bacteria (antibiotics needed) and sometimes by viruses (antibiotics do not work on viruses), so antibiotics are needed only sometimes.
Multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis are autoimmune diseases, not caused by pathogens, so antibiotics are not needed.

questions.question: Which row of the table describes each of drugs J, K and L from the graph?
questions.answer: B: drug J is not an antibiotic, drug K is a bacteriostatic antibiotic and drug L is a bactericidal antibiotic.
steps: With drug J the number of bacteria rises quickly, so it has no antibacterial effect (not an antibiotic).
With drug K the number of bacteria rises only very slightly, so growth is stopped but the bacteria are not killed: bacteriostatic.
With drug L the number of bacteria falls steadily, so the bacteria are being killed: bactericidal.

questions.question: Explain the role of gut flora in protecting the body from infection.
questions.answer: Gut flora compete with pathogens for space and nutrients, and produce substances that inhibit pathogens.
steps: Normal gut flora occupy binding sites on the gut wall, blocking pathogens from attaching.
They compete with pathogens for nutrients and space.
Some gut flora produce acids or antimicrobial substances that inhibit pathogens.
They also help stimulate the development of the immune system.

questions.question: Explain why antibiotics can affect gut flora.
questions.answer: Antibiotics kill or inhibit the bacteria of gut flora as well as the pathogens, because gut flora are also bacteria.
steps: Gut flora are bacteria, which are susceptible to antibiotics.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill many types of bacteria, including the beneficial ones.
Killing gut flora removes competition, so resistant or harmful species may grow.
This reduces the protective effect of gut flora against infection.

questions.question: The number of type A bacteria in gut flora without antibiotics is 6 000 000. Estimate the number of type B, in standard form.
questions.answer: About 1 x 10^7
steps: On the 'no antibiotic' pie chart, the sector for type A is about 63 degrees and the sector for type B is about 106 degrees.
Number of type B = 1.7 x 6 000 000 = 1.0 x 10^7 (about 1 x 10^7).

questions.question: Deduce the effects of antibiotics P, Q and R on gut flora, using the diagrams.
questions.answer: P and Q greatly reduce the diversity of gut flora, leaving mainly one type, whereas R has little effect on the types and proportions.
steps: Antibiotic P: only three types remain (one type makes up about 75%), so most types are killed and diversity is much reduced.
Antibiotic Q: more types remain than with P but they are in very small proportions and one type is about 75% of the total, so diversity is also greatly reduced.

Antibiotic R: the types and proportions are almost the same as with no antibiotic, so R has little or no effect on gut flora (it may be narrow-spectrum); the charts show proportions, not the total number of bacteria.

questions.question: Explain why the development of Castaneroxy A is an example of an 'evolutionary race' between humans and the pathogen.
questions.answer: Humans develop new drugs in response to pathogens evolving resistance, and the pathogen then evolves further resistance, so the race continues.
steps: MRSA evolves resistance to antibiotics such as methicillin through natural selection.
Humans respond by developing new drugs such as Castaneroxy A.
The pathogen may then evolve resistance to the new drug through further mutations.
So both humans and pathogens keep evolving in response to each other.

questions.question: Explain why it is important that Castaneroxy A does not affect the natural skin flora.
questions.answer: Skin flora protect the body by competing with pathogens, so killing them would let MRSA colonise and cause infection.
steps: Skin flora occupy space and use nutrients, so pathogens cannot colonise easily.
If the drug killed skin flora, this competition would be removed.
MRSA could then colonise the skin more easily and cause infection.
So the drug must target only the pathogen.

questions.question: Suggest how weakening the MRSA bacteria could help the recovery of a patient.
questions.answer: Weakened bacteria are easier for phagocytes and the immune system to destroy, and they produce fewer toxins, so the infection clears faster.
steps: Weakened bacteria are less able to resist phagocytosis and immune attack.
White blood cells can engulf and destroy them more easily.
Fewer toxins are produced, so less tissue damage and inflammation occurs.
The infection is cleared more quickly and the patient recovers.

questions.question: Explain why the investigation included a group treated with only the solvent.
questions.answer: The solvent control shows that any change in infection size is due to Castaneroxy A and not to the solvent.
steps: The solvent is used to dissolve Castaneroxy A, so it could affect the infection on its own.
A group treated with only solvent shows the effect of the solvent alone.
Comparing it with the drug groups isolates the effect of Castaneroxy A.
This makes the investigation a valid, controlled test.

questions.question: Determine the effect that Castaneroxy A has on the mean size of skin infections, using the graph.
questions.answer: Castaneroxy A reduces the mean size of the skin infection at both concentrations, and 50 ug per cm^3 reduces it much more than 10 ug per cm^3 (peak about 0.05 cm^2 against about 0.57 cm^2, compared with 1.13 cm^2 with solvent only).
steps: With solvent only, the mean size of infection rises to a peak of about 1.13 cm^2 at 6 days and falls to about 0.28 cm^2 by 14 days.
With 10 ug per cm^3 Castaneroxy A the peak is about 0.57 cm^2 at 6 days (about 50% lower than the control), falling to about 0.05 cm^2 at 14 days (about 80% lower).

With 50 ug per cm^3 the infection stays very small, below about 0.07 cm^2 at all times, a reduction of about 95% at the peak and about 100% by 12 to 14 days, so a higher concentration is much more effective; the error bars do not overlap with the control after day 3, so the differences are probably significant.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of leaves, in kg, needed to produce 1 dm3 of Castaneroxy A at 50 g per cm3, given the leaves contain 0.0019% by mass (nearest kg).
questions.answer: About 2 631 579 kg of leaves (2.63 x 10^6 kg).
steps: 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3, so mass of Castaneroxy A = 50 g/cm3 x 1000 cm3 = 50 000 g = 50 kg.
0.0019% = 0.0019 / 100 = 1.9 x 10^-5 as a fraction of leaf mass.
Mass of leaves = 50 kg / 1.9 x 10^-5 = 2 631 579 kg.
Rounded to the nearest kilogram this is 2 631 579 kg.

questions.question: Name the two other characteristics of inflammation besides heat and redness.
questions.answer: Swelling and pain.
steps: Inflammation is characterised by redness, heat, swelling and pain.
So the two other characteristics are swelling and pain.
These are the classic characteristics of inflammation with heat and redness.
Swelling and pain are the other two signs of inflammation.

questions.question: Explain how heat helps the body respond to infection.
questions.answer: Heat speeds up the activity of phagocytes and enzymes and slows pathogen growth.
steps: Raised temperature increases the metabolic rate and enzyme activity of phagocytes.
This allows white blood cells to act faster against pathogens.
Many pathogens grow less well at higher temperatures, so their growth is slowed.
Heat also increases blood flow, bringing more phagocytes to the infection.

questions.question: Describe how interferon helps the body respond to infection.
questions.answer: Virus-infected cells release interferon, which binds to neighbouring cells and makes them produce antiviral proteins that inhibit virus replication.
steps: Cells infected with a virus release interferon.
Interferon binds to receptors on neighbouring uninfected cells.
These cells then make antiviral proteins that block viral replication.
So the spread of the virus to other cells is slowed.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the changes in antibody concentration in the blood plasma after the first infection and the second infection, using the graph.
questions.answer: Both show a rise in antibody concentration and then a fall, but after the second infection the rise starts sooner, is much faster and reaches a much higher peak (about 2.5 times higher) than after the first infection.
steps: Similarity: after both infections the antibody concentration rises to a peak and then falls.

Difference: after the first infection there is a lag before the concentration rises slowly, to a lower peak; after the second infection the rise starts immediately and is very steep, reaching a much higher peak.
Reason: memory B cells formed after the first infection respond rapidly to the same antigen, so plasma cells make a lot of antibody quickly (the secondary response).

questions.question: Estimate the percentage composition of oligosaccharides in colostrum from the charts.
questions.answer: About 60%
steps: The pie chart for colostrum has three sectors: oligosaccharides (the largest), protein and fat.
Measuring the angle for oligosaccharides gives about 216 degrees, since fat is about 80 degrees and protein about 58 degrees.
Percentage = 216 / 360 x 100 = 60% (accept about 55 to 65%).

questions.question: Describe two conclusions about the gut flora of babies fed breast milk or another milk, from the graph.
questions.answer: Babies fed breast milk have a higher proportion of Bifidobacterium and Bacteroides, and a lower proportion of Enterococcus, Streptococcus and Veillonella, than those fed another milk.
steps: Conclusion 1: Bifidobacterium is the most common type in both groups, but the proportion is higher in the breast milk group (about 1.4 times as high).

Conclusion 2: Bacteroides is much more common in breast-fed babies (about 8 times as high), whereas Enterococcus, Streptococcus and Veillonella are less common in breast-fed babies than in the other group.
So breast milk (probably the oligosaccharides) changes the types of gut flora.

questions.question: Explain the importance of healthy gut flora in preventing infection in a developing baby.
questions.answer: Healthy gut flora compete with pathogens for nutrients and space and help stimulate the immune system.
steps: Gut flora occupy the gut surface, so pathogens have fewer places to attach.
They compete with pathogens for nutrients.
They produce substances that inhibit pathogens and help train the developing immune system.
Healthy gut flora therefore supports protection from infection in babies.

questions.question: Explain the possible advantages of using oligosaccharides from breast milk instead of antibiotics to treat GBS infections.
questions.answer: Bacteria are less likely to develop resistance to oligosaccharides, and they are natural and less likely to damage the gut flora.
steps: Bacteria are increasingly resistant to antibiotics, so a new antimicrobial is needed.
Oligosaccharides are natural molecules, so resistance is less likely to evolve quickly.
They may act more specifically against GBS and spare the beneficial gut flora.
Using them avoids the side effects and gut damage caused by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

questions.question: How many of the three statements about lambda phage are correct (A 0, B 1, C 2, D 3)?
questions.answer: D: 3 (DNA genetic material, complex capsid, and genetic material codes for J protein).
steps: Lambda phage has DNA as its genetic material, so the first statement is correct.
Lambda phage has a complex capsid (head and tail), so the second statement is correct.
Its DNA codes for the J protein used to attach to the host cell, so the third statement is correct.
All three statements are correct, so option D is the answer.

questions.question: Describe the role of the lambda phage J protein, using the diagram.
questions.answer: The J protein binds to maltoporin on the E. coli surface, attaching the phage to the host cell so its DNA can be injected.
steps: The J protein is on the phage tail and fits a receptor on the host cell surface.
In the diagram it is attached to maltoporin, a protein on the E. coli outer membrane.
This attachment holds the phage to the host cell.
The phage can then inject its DNA into the bacterium to begin infection.

questions.question: Give one reason why sugars are important to E. coli.
questions.answer: Sugars such as glucose are a source of energy for respiration.
steps: Glucose is respired to release energy in the form of ATP.
Sugars also provide carbon atoms for building other organic molecules.
Sugars are essential nutrients for the growth and metabolism of E. coli.
Glucose also provides carbon for building new cell material.

questions.question: Discuss how E. coli and lambda phage could interact and develop in their evolutionary race for existence, using the information given.
questions.answer: Random mutations in the lam gene change maltoporin so phage cannot bind; phage mutations in the J protein restore binding, and selection drives this cycle.
steps: Random mutation in the lam gene can change the maltoporin shape so the J protein no longer binds it.
E. coli with this mutation survive phage infection and reproduce, so the mutant allele becomes more common.
Phage with mutations in the J protein that can bind the altered maltoporin survive and reproduce.
The phage population then has an advantage, so E. coli must mutate again to escape infection.
Each cycle of mutation and natural selection in both species drives an evolutionary arms race.
The arms race continues as long as both species keep producing variants that are selected.

questions.question: Describe how the viral RNA of dengue virus is translated on the endoplasmic reticulum into one polyprotein.
questions.answer: Ribosomes bind the viral mRNA; tRNA molecules bring amino acids matched to codons, and peptide bonds join them to form the polyprotein.
steps: Ribosomes attach to the viral RNA on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
tRNA molecules with anticodons complementary to each codon bring specific amino acids.
Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds catalysed by the ribosome, lengthening the chain.
The ribosome reaches a stop codon and releases the single long polyprotein chain.

questions.question: Suggest how an inhibitor of the protease enzyme NS3B2 could result in fewer viruses being produced.
questions.answer: The protease cuts the polyprotein into functional proteins; with the inhibitor, these proteins are not released, so virus replication and assembly is reduced.
steps: NS3B2 protease cuts the polyprotein at specific sites to release functional viral proteins.
An inhibitor blocks the active site of the protease, so cleavage cannot occur.
Without separated proteins, the enzymes and structural proteins needed for replication are not active.
So fewer new viruses are assembled and released from the infected cell.

questions.question: Explain how higher platelet and white blood cell counts may have helped recovery from dengue virus infection.
questions.answer: Platelets prevent bleeding by helping blood clot, and white blood cells fight the virus through phagocytosis and killing infected cells.
steps: Platelets are needed for blood clotting, so higher counts reduce bleeding, a serious complication of dengue.
Higher platelet counts help maintain blood pressure and prevent haemorrhage.
White blood cells such as macrophages and lymphocytes engulf and destroy virus particles.
T killer cells and antibodies from white blood cells destroy virus-infected cells, reducing viral spread.

questions.question: Describe two advantages of using Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes to control dengue.
questions.answer: Wolbachia are passed to future generations, so the control is self-sustaining; and it does not harm the mosquitoes or need insecticides.
steps: Wolbachia are inherited by offspring, so they spread through the mosquito population over time.
The bacteria do not harm the mosquitoes, so the control does not reduce the mosquito population directly.
Less dependence on insecticides avoids resistance in mosquitoes and environmental damage.
Mosquitoes are not harmed, so they can carry Wolbachia continuously.

questions.question: Describe how skin flora protect the body from infection.
questions.answer: Skin flora compete with pathogens for space and nutrients, and some produce substances that inhibit pathogens.
steps: Skin flora occupy space on the skin surface, so pathogens cannot attach easily.
They compete with pathogens for nutrients.
Some skin bacteria produce acids or antimicrobial substances that kill or inhibit pathogens.
These mechanisms prevent infection without needing an immune response.

questions.question: Give one other way in which the skin protects the body from infection.
questions.answer: It acts as a physical barrier of dead, keratinised cells that pathogens cannot penetrate.
steps: The outer layer of dead keratinised cells is a physical barrier to microbes.
Sweat and sebum also create an acidic surface that inhibits microbes.
Sweat and sebum also create an acidic surface that inhibits microbes.
The outer layer of dead cells is a barrier that most microbes cannot cross.

questions.question: Describe three conclusions that could be made from the graph of bacteria groups on the skin of men of different ages.
questions.answer: Teenagers have the most Firmicutes (about 21%) and Actinobacteria (about 30%), whereas middle-aged and elderly men are dominated by Proteobacteria (about 87-88%); middle-aged and elderly men are very similar.
steps: Conclusion 1: Proteobacteria are the largest group in all three age groups, but make up only about 46% in teenagers compared with about 88% in the middle aged and about 86% in the elderly.
Conclusion 2: Firmicutes fall from about 21% in teenagers to about 2% in the middle aged and elderly, and Actinobacteria fall from about 30% to about 9-11%.

Conclusion 3: Middle-aged and elderly men have almost the same skin flora, with the elderly having slightly more Actinobacteria (about 11% against 9%) and slightly less Proteobacteria; the 'others' group is a small percentage (about 1 to 3%) at every age, so most change occurs between teenage years and middle age.

questions.question: Describe how this study should have been designed to collect valid data.
questions.answer: Use a large random sample of men in each age group, and control variables such as hygiene and sampling site, with repeats.
steps: Use a large sample size in each age group so results are representative.
Select participants randomly to avoid bias.
Control variables such as washing, hygiene and the sampling site on the skin.
Use the same sampling and culturing method for every person, with repeats to check reliability.
