questions.question: Describe the role of macrophages in the non-specific response to bacteria that get through the skin.
questions.answer: Macrophages engulf bacteria by phagocytosis and digest them in lysosomes.
steps: Macrophages engulf bacteria by phagocytosis, surrounding them in a vesicle.
Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle and digest the bacteria with enzymes.
Macrophages also release chemicals that cause inflammation and attract more phagocytes.
Phagocytosis is a non-specific response, as it does not need antigen recognition.

questions.question: Describe the role of macrophages in the immune response to these bacteria.
questions.answer: Macrophages present bacterial antigens on MHC class II to T helper cells, which activate the specific immune response.
steps: After engulfing bacteria, macrophages display bacterial antigens on their surface bound to MHC class II.
T helper cells with complementary receptors bind to the antigen-MHC complex.
Binding activates the T helper cells, which then activate B cells and T killer cells.
This links the non-specific response of macrophages to the specific immune response.

questions.question: Which pair of viruses have an envelope (options A to D)?
questions.answer: A: Ebola virus and HIV.
steps: Ebola virus and HIV both have an outer lipid envelope taken from the host cell membrane.
TMV and lambda phage do not have an envelope.
So option A is the correct pair.
Option A is the only pair in which both viruses have an envelope.

questions.question: Which virus has a complex capsid structure (options A to D)?
questions.answer: C: lambda phage.
steps: Complex capsids have a head and a tail or other extra structures.
Lambda phage has a complex capsid with a head and tail.
Ebola is helical, HIV is icosahedral (conical), and TMV is helical.
Option C (lambda phage) is the only virus with a complex capsid.

questions.question: How many of Ebola virus, HIV, lambda phage and TMV are RNA viruses (options A to D)?
steps: Ebola virus, HIV and TMV all have RNA as their genetic material.
Lambda phage has double-stranded DNA, so it is not an RNA virus.
So three viruses are RNA viruses: option C.
Option C is the count of RNA viruses.

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the base sequence of the positive RNA strand complementary to the given negative strand.
questions.answer: U G G U U C C G C
steps: The positive strand is complementary to the negative strand, using RNA base pairing.
A pairs with U (there is no thymine in RNA), C with G, G with C.
Negative A C C A A G G C G gives positive U G G U U C C G C.

questions.question: Explain why a positive RNA strand has to be made from the negative RNA strand of the rabies virus.
questions.answer: The positive strand acts as mRNA for translation into viral proteins and as a template for making new negative RNA genomes.
steps: The negative RNA strand cannot be read by ribosomes, so it cannot be translated directly.
A positive RNA strand is made by RNA polymerase using the negative strand as a template.
The positive strand acts as mRNA, so ribosomes make viral proteins from it.
It also serves as a template to make more negative RNA genomes for new virus particles.

questions.question: Explain why doctors were worried that the person bitten by a lemur had left treatment too long for rabies to be successful.
questions.answer: Rabies travels along nerves to the brain, and once symptoms appear the disease is almost always fatal, so treatment must start early.
steps: Rabies virus enters through the bite and replicates in muscle cells near the wound.
It then travels along neurones (retrograde transport) toward the central nervous system.
Once the virus reaches the brain, it causes severe symptoms that cannot be stopped by treatment.
Delayed treatment means the virus may already have reached the brain, so treatment is unlikely to work.

questions.question: State the relationship between optical density and the size of the microorganisms.
questions.answer: The larger the microorganism, the higher the optical density for the same number of cells, because larger cells absorb and scatter more light.
steps: Light is absorbed and scattered by cells in the culture.
Larger cells, such as yeast, scatter more light per cell than smaller bacteria.
So larger microorganisms give a higher optical density at the same cell number.
So the size of the microorganism changes the optical density per cell.

questions.question: Calculate how many times more bacterial cells there are than yeast cells if both samples have an optical density of 1.0 a.u.
steps: On the graph, at an optical density of 1.0 a.u., the bacterial cells number about 12.5 x 10^6 per cm^3.
The yeast cells at an optical density of 1.0 a.u. number about 0.4 x 10^6 per cm^3.
Ratio = 12.5 / 0.4 = 31, so about 30 times more bacterial cells.

questions.question: State the relationship between the number of bacterial cells and the optical density.
questions.answer: Optical density increases as the number of bacterial cells increases (a positive relationship, linear at low concentrations).
steps: The more cells in the sample, the more light is absorbed or scattered.
So optical density rises with cell number.
The rise is roughly linear at low cell concentrations and levels off at high concentrations.
The relationship is roughly linear, so calibration curves are needed for accuracy.

questions.question: Suggest why using optical density is more accurate at lower concentrations of cells, using the diagram of light passing through the culture.
questions.answer: At low concentrations the cells are spread out, so light is absorbed in proportion to cell number; at high concentrations cells shade each other and the curve levels off.
steps: At low cell concentrations each cell absorbs or scatters light independently.
So the optical density is directly proportional to cell number.
At high concentrations cells block light from each other, so most light is absorbed.
The detector then cannot tell the difference between high densities, so the reading is less accurate.

questions.question: A medium was inoculated with 6 x 10^3 bacteria and at the end had 1.2 x 10^7 bacteria. Using k = 0.963 and Nt = N0 e^(kt), calculate the incubation time t.
steps: Use the exponential growth equation Nt = N0 x e^(kt) (the standard form for this equation).
Rearrange: t = ln(Nt / N0) / k.

questions.question: Explain why one calibration curve cannot be used to determine the growth of all microorganisms, using the information and your own knowledge.
questions.answer: Different microorganisms differ in size, shape and structure, so the same optical density corresponds to different cell numbers; each species needs its own calibration curve.
steps: Bacteria and yeast cells differ in size, shape and cell structure (prokaryote versus eukaryote).
Larger or more complex cells scatter and absorb light differently, so one cell gives a different optical density.
So the same optical density reading corresponds to a different number of cells for each species (as shown by the two calibration curves).
Cell colour or pigment content also changes light absorption, so the optical density per cell changes.
Some microorganisms form filaments or clumps, which scatter light differently from single cells.
So a calibration curve must be made for each species or type of microorganism being studied.

questions.question: State two precautions that should be taken to ensure only one type of bacteria is grown in the culture.
questions.answer: Use sterile equipment and media, and flame the loop and bottle necks so no other microbes contaminate the culture.
steps: Sterilise all equipment (for example by flaming) before and after use.
Use sterile agar and Petri dishes so no unwanted microbes are already present.
Work near a Bunsen flame and keep lids on dishes to exclude airborne microbes.
Both precautions help make sure the culture contains only one species.

questions.question: How much more antibiotic is in part B3 than in part B2 of the mast ring (options A to D)?
questions.answer: C: 50.0 times.
steps: Part B3 has 0.5 mg = 500 ug of antibiotic B; part B2 has 10 ug of antibiotic B.
500 / 10 = 50, so B3 has 50.0 times as much.

questions.question: Explain how the results shown in the diagram can help a doctor decide how to prescribe antibiotics to a patient infected with this bacteria.
questions.answer: The antibiotic with the largest clear zone of inhibition is most effective, and the smallest effective mass shows the dose needed.
steps: A clear zone of inhibition shows where the antibiotic has stopped bacterial growth.
The larger the diameter of the zone, the more effective the antibiotic against this bacteria.
The lowest mass that still gives a clear zone shows the minimum effective dose.
A doctor would choose the most effective antibiotic at the lowest effective dose, avoiding resistant strains.

questions.question: Describe the role of the viral genome of an Ebola virus.
questions.answer: The viral genome carries the genetic information that codes for the viral proteins needed to make new viruses.
steps: The viral genome is RNA that contains the genetic code for all viral proteins.
It is used as a template to make viral mRNA and new viral genomes.
So it controls the production of new virus particles inside the host cell.
The genome therefore determines which viral proteins the virus can make.

questions.question: Describe the role of the glycoproteins of an Ebola virus.
questions.answer: The glycoproteins on the envelope bind to receptors on host cells, allowing the virus to attach and enter.
steps: Glycoproteins protrude from the viral envelope.
They fit complementary receptors on the surface of host cells.
Binding allows the virus to attach and be taken into the cell by endocytosis or membrane fusion.
Glycoproteins are therefore needed for the virus to infect new cells.

questions.question: Explain why the structure of the Ebola virus includes RNA polymerase.
questions.answer: Ebola has an RNA genome, so it needs its own RNA polymerase to transcribe its RNA into mRNA, because host cells cannot use viral RNA directly.
steps: Ebola virus has RNA as its genetic material.
Host cells normally make mRNA from DNA, not from RNA templates.
So the virus carries RNA polymerase to copy its RNA into mRNA and new genomes inside the host cell.
So the virus carries its own RNA polymerase into the host cell.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term virus assembly, using Ebola as an example.
questions.answer: Virus assembly is the joining together of viral genome, capsid proteins and enzymes to form new virus particles, which then bud from the host cell.
steps: Newly made viral RNA, structural proteins and enzymes are brought together inside the host cell.
VP40 and VP24 help the proteins and genome come together to form the nucleocapsid.
The new virus particle then buds out through the host cell membrane, taking an envelope with it.
Assembly is followed by budding out of the host cell to release new viruses.

questions.question: Explain why the structure of the Ebola virus includes VP35, which inhibits the production of interferon by host cells.
questions.answer: Interferon triggers antiviral defences in neighbouring cells, so VP35 stops this response and lets the virus replicate.
steps: Infected cells normally release interferon to warn neighbouring cells.
Interferon causes neighbouring cells to produce antiviral proteins that block virus replication.
VP35 blocks interferon production, so the antiviral defence is not triggered.
This allows the Ebola virus to replicate and spread more easily.

questions.question: What type of molecule is mycolic acid (options A to D)?
questions.answer: B: fatty acid.
steps: Mycolic acids are long-chain fatty acids that form part of the mycobacterial cell wall.
They are not carbohydrates, nucleic acids or polypeptides.
So the answer is option B.
Mycolic acids are long-chain fatty acids that form part of the waxy cell wall.

questions.question: Suggest why antibiotic E is effective only when M. tuberculosis bacteria are dividing.
questions.answer: Antibiotic E targets a process, such as cell wall synthesis, that occurs only when the bacteria are growing and dividing.
steps: Some antibiotics block synthesis of new cell wall material.
Cell wall synthesis only happens during cell growth and division.
So the drug has no effect on non-dividing bacteria.
This restricts the action of the drug to periods of active growth.

questions.question: Explain why antibiotic J could result in an increase in antigen presentation by macrophages.
questions.answer: Antibiotic J kills the bacteria, releasing more bacterial antigens that macrophages engulf and present on MHC class II.
steps: Antibiotic J kills M. tuberculosis, so more bacteria are destroyed.
Macrophages engulf the dead or damaged bacteria by phagocytosis.
They digest the bacteria and display the antigens on their surface on MHC class II molecules.
More antigen presentation activates more T helper cells.

questions.question: Explain how antibiotic P could affect M. tuberculosis, using the table of antibiotics.
questions.answer: P prevents synthesis of fatty acids, so the bacteria cannot make mycolic acids for their cell wall, which makes them more vulnerable to lysozyme, dehydration and polar antibiotics, and slows growth.
steps: Antibiotic P activates an enzyme that inhibits the synthesis of fatty acids, and mycolic acids are long-chain fatty acids, so fewer mycolic acids are made.
Without mycolic acid the cell wall is weaker and less protective, so the bacteria are more easily damaged by lysozyme, by dehydration and by polar (hydrophilic) antibiotics.
New cell walls and membranes cannot be made for new cells, so the bacteria cannot divide or grow properly, and so they are killed or their number falls.

questions.question: Explain how antibiotic R could affect M. tuberculosis, using the table of antibiotics.
questions.answer: R binds to the active site of RNA polymerase, so transcription stops, and no mRNA, enzymes or other proteins are made, so the bacteria cannot grow or divide.
steps: Antibiotic R is a competitive inhibitor: it binds to the active site of RNA polymerase, so the enzyme cannot bind to the DNA template and make mRNA.
Without mRNA there is no translation, so the bacteria cannot make new proteins such as enzymes (for example for cell wall synthesis, DNA replication and respiration).
So the bacteria cannot grow, repair themselves or divide, and the bacterial population falls; it acts on the bacterial RNA polymerase and so has little effect on human cells.

questions.question: Explain why taking a combination of antibiotics for several months could increase the resistance of M. tuberculosis to these antibiotics.
questions.answer: Random mutations give some bacteria resistance; long treatment selects these survivors, which then multiply and pass on resistance.
steps: Random mutations may give some M. tuberculosis resistance to one or more antibiotics.
Antibiotic treatment kills sensitive bacteria, so resistant mutants survive (natural selection).
Over several months the resistant bacteria multiply and become the dominant population.
Incomplete courses or drug combinations can leave resistant survivors, increasing resistance.

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of children to women to men who developed TB, from 1.2 million children, 3.2 million women and 5.6 million men.
steps: Divide each value by the smallest value, 1.2 million (or by 0.4 million).
So the ratio children : women : men = 3 : 8 : 14.
Ratios are simplified by dividing by the smallest value.

questions.question: Explain how infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis may result in death.
questions.answer: Bacteria destroy lung tissue and cause inflammation, reducing gas exchange until the lungs fail; the disease can also spread to other organs.
steps: M. tuberculosis multiplies inside macrophages and lung tissue, forming granulomas.
The infection and inflammation damage the alveoli, so less surface area is available for gas exchange.
Reduced oxygen uptake and respiratory failure can cause death if untreated.
The infection can also spread to other organs, causing organ failure.

questions.question: Explain why the macrophages had to be treated to stimulate IL-1 release in this investigation.
questions.answer: The treatment is a positive control showing that macrophages can release IL-1, so any lower release in infected cells is due to M. tuberculosis.
steps: Without stimulation, macrophages release little IL-1 whether or not they are infected.
Stimulating the macrophages shows that they can release IL-1 normally (positive control).
Comparing infected and uninfected stimulated macrophages shows the inhibition caused by M. tuberculosis.
So the inhibitory effect of M. tuberculosis on IL-1 release can be identified.

questions.question: Explain how the steps in the ELISA result in the identification of IL-1, using the diagram.
questions.answer: A specific antibody captures IL-1, a second enzyme-linked antibody binds it, and the substrate produces a colour change that shows its presence.
steps: The well is coated with antibodies specific to IL-1, which capture the IL-1 in the sample.
After washing, a second enzyme-linked antibody binds to a different site on the IL-1 (sandwich).
Adding the enzyme's substrate produces a coloured product only where the enzyme is bound.
The intensity of colour is measured, showing the amount of IL-1 present.

questions.question: Describe how optical methods (turbidity) can be used to compare the growth rates of mutant and unmutated M. tuberculosis populations.
questions.answer: Grow equal starting numbers of mutant and unmutated bacteria in identical broth; at regular time intervals measure the absorbance (turbidity) of samples in a colorimeter zeroed with sterile broth, where more cells absorb more light; then plot absorbance (or cell number from a calibration curve) against time and compare the gradients of the exponential phases.
steps: Inoculate equal numbers of mutant and unmutated bacteria into the same volume of identical sterile broth, kept at the same temperature.
Zero (calibrate) the colorimeter or spectrophotometer using a cuvette of sterile, uninoculated broth.
At regular time intervals remove a sample from each culture and measure its absorbance (or percentage transmission) of light.
The more bacterial cells there are, the more turbid the culture, so the higher the absorbance (less light transmitted).
Convert absorbance to cell number using a calibration curve if needed, and plot absorbance against time for both populations.
Compare the gradients of the exponential (log) phases: the steeper gradient shows the faster growth rate.

questions.question: Suggest how this protein, released by M. tuberculosis, could be used to develop a treatment for TB.
questions.answer: Develop a drug or antibody that blocks the protein so the macrophages can be activated to kill the bacteria.
steps: The protein suppresses macrophage activation when released by the bacteria.
A drug or antibody that blocks or neutralises the protein would stop this suppression.
Macrophages could then be activated to destroy the bacteria.
Blocking the protein would stop it suppressing macrophage activation.

questions.question: How many of the organelles labelled in the fungal cell diagram have membranes (options A to D)?
steps: The membrane-bound organelles labelled are the nuclei (double membrane), the mitochondria (double membrane) and the Golgi apparatus (single membrane): 3.
The cell wall, ribosomes, glycogen granules and cytoplasm have no membrane, and the cell membrane is not an organelle.

questions.question: Explain why fungi are not classified as bacteria, plants or animals.
questions.answer: Fungi are eukaryotes with membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus (unlike bacteria), have chitin cell walls (unlike plants), and absorb food externally (unlike animals).
steps: Fungi are eukaryotic, with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, unlike prokaryotic bacteria.
Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose as in plants or peptidoglycan as in bacteria.
Fungi lack chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise like plants.
Fungi digest food externally and absorb it, unlike animals which ingest food.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between the number of aminopenicillin prescriptions and the percentage of E. coli resistant to aminopenicillin, using the graph.
questions.answer: There is a positive correlation with a time lag: resistance peaks in March to April, about 1 to 2 months after the peak of prescriptions in January to February, and both fall to a minimum in July to September, then rise again.
steps: When many prescriptions are issued (January to February), antibiotic use gives selection pressure: sensitive bacteria are killed but resistant E. coli survive and reproduce, so the percentage resistant rises, to a peak in March to April.

When the number of prescriptions falls (to the lowest in July), there is less selection pressure, so non-resistant bacteria are no longer killed and increase, so the percentage of resistant E. coli falls (to a minimum from July to September).

The change in resistance lags behind the change in prescriptions by about 1 to 2 months, because it takes time for the bacteria to reproduce and for the proportions to change, and for the resistance alleles to spread (including by horizontal transfer of plasmids).
When prescriptions rise again from July, resistance rises about two months later, so the two curves follow the same pattern.

questions.question: Explain why the results of this survey are a cause for concern.
questions.answer: Misuse of antibiotics (to satisfy patient pressure and without knowing if needed) increases selection for antibiotic-resistant bacteria, so infections become harder to treat and fewer antibiotics are left that work.
steps: Prescribing antibiotics for viral infections (the 70% unsure and 49% not knowing if necessary) is a waste because antibiotics have no effect on viruses.
Unnecessary use puts selection pressure on bacteria, so resistant strains such as MRSA survive, reproduce and pass on the resistance alleles, and resistance spreads in the population.
Then fewer infections can be treated, so illness and deaths and costs rise; 90% felt under pressure and 44% prescribed to get a patient to leave, which means decisions are not made on medical need.

questions.question: Describe how a vaccine results in active immunity.
questions.answer: The vaccine contains antigens that trigger B cells and T cells to divide and produce antibodies and memory cells.
steps: The vaccine contains antigens (dead, attenuated or fragments) that the immune system recognises as foreign.
Macrophages present the antigen to T helper cells, which activate B cells with complementary receptors (clonal selection).
Activated B cells divide by mitosis and differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
Memory B and T cells are also formed, giving a faster response if the real pathogen infects later.

questions.question: Identify three conclusions from the results of the vaccine attitude survey, using the graph.
questions.answer: In every income group trust in scientists is highest in those who agree that vaccines are safe and lowest in those who disagree; trust falls as income rises, and the gap between the agree and disagree groups is bigger in high-income groups.
steps: Conclusion 1: in all four income groups, people who agree vaccines are safe have the highest trust in scientists, and those who disagree have the lowest, with 'neither' in between.
Conclusion 2: trust in scientists is lower as income rises for all three groups, for example 'agree' falls from about 238 to 217 on the vertical scale, and 'disagree' from about 187 to 142.
Conclusion 3: the difference between those who agree and those who disagree is greater in the high-income group (about 35% lower) than in the low-income group (about 21% lower).

questions.question: Suggest one reason for the different attitudes of these people to vaccines.
questions.answer: Differences in income or access to reliable information affect how much people trust scientists and vaccine safety.
steps: People with different incomes have different access to healthcare and reliable information.
Less access to reliable information can lead to doubts about vaccine safety.
So attitudes towards vaccines vary across different income groups.
This is one plausible reason, linked to the survey data on trust and income.

questions.question: Suggest why vaccination is more successful when a greater proportion of people are vaccinated.
questions.answer: Fewer susceptible people remain, so the pathogen has fewer hosts to infect and cannot spread easily (herd immunity).
steps: Vaccinated people cannot easily catch or pass on the pathogen.
When most people are vaccinated, the pathogen cannot find enough susceptible hosts.
Even non-vaccinated people are protected because the spread of infection is reduced (herd immunity).
Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.question: Which virus can infect bacteria (options A to D)?
questions.answer: C: lambda phage.
steps: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria.
Lambda phage is a bacteriophage that infects E. coli.
Ebola and HIV infect animals and TMV infects plants.
Lambda phage infects E. coli, so it is a bacteriophage.

questions.question: Describe the role of channel proteins in the facilitated diffusion of lysins across bacterial membranes.
questions.answer: Channel proteins form a hydrophilic pore through the membrane, allowing polar lysins to pass down their concentration gradient without energy.
steps: Channel proteins form a water-filled, hydrophilic pore through the phospholipid bilayer.
Polar lysins cannot cross the hydrophobic bilayer, so they use the channel.
They pass down their concentration gradient by facilitated diffusion, needing no ATP.
Channels let lysins pass through without using energy.

questions.question: Explain how the primary structure and the tertiary structure of holins determine the properties of these channel proteins.
questions.answer: The primary structure sets the sequence of amino acids, which folds into a tertiary shape with hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions that form and line the channel.
steps: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, which is coded by the holin gene.
The sequence determines which R groups are hydrophilic or hydrophobic.
These amino acids fold by hydrogen, ionic and hydrophobic bonds into the tertiary structure.
Hydrophobic parts face the lipid bilayer and hydrophilic parts line the central channel, giving it its properties.

questions.question: Explain the role of lysins in the lytic cycle, given that lysins break down the bacterial cell wall.
questions.answer: Lysins break down the bacterial cell wall so the cell bursts (lyses), releasing the new virus particles.
steps: Lysins digest the peptidoglycan of the bacterial cell wall.
With the wall weakened, the bacterial cell lyses under osmotic pressure.

questions.question: State the difference between a bacteriostatic antibiotic and a bactericidal antibiotic.
questions.answer: A bacteriostatic antibiotic stops bacteria growing or dividing, while a bactericidal antibiotic kills them.

questions.question: Suggest why low methane concentrations cannot support the growth of some methanotrophs, such as methanotroph A.
questions.answer: Methanotroph A needs a minimum methane concentration to obtain enough carbon and energy to grow.
steps: Methanotrophs use methane as their energy and carbon source.
Below a minimum concentration, there is not enough methane to supply the energy needed for growth.
So the methanotroph cannot grow at low methane concentrations.
Methanotroph A cannot grow below this threshold concentration.

questions.question: Suggest why the scientists analysed the cultures of methanotroph B for the production of nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: To check that the bacteria do not produce other greenhouse gases as waste, which would offset the benefit of removing methane.
steps: Methanotrophs convert methane to CO2 and biomass, and some may produce nitrous oxide.
If methanotroph B produces nitrous oxide or extra CO2, it could add to global warming.
So the analysis checks whether it is a suitable method for reducing greenhouse gases.
Checking gas output confirms the method does not add greenhouse gases.

questions.question: Explain how retroviruses introduce ERVs into human cells and how ancient ERVs can be transmitted to offspring in families.
questions.answer: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the viral RNA and integrase inserts it into the host genome as a provirus; if inserted into germ-line cells, it is passed to offspring.
steps: The retrovirus enters the cell and reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into double-stranded DNA.
Integrase inserts the viral DNA into the host chromosome as a provirus.
If infection happens in germ-line cells (sperm or egg precursors), the provirus is present in the gametes.
Offspring inherit the ERV in every cell, so it is passed through many generations in families.
Over millions of years the ERV sequences accumulate mutations and remain as part of the genome.
So ancient ERVs are found in human DNA today.

questions.question: Explain how epigenetic regulation prevents the synthesis of the viral envelope proteins coded by ERVs in normal cells.
questions.answer: DNA methylation and histone modification make chromatin tightly packed, so RNA polymerase cannot transcribe the ERV genes and no protein is made.
steps: Methylation of the DNA of the ERV gene adds methyl groups to cytosine bases.
Histone proteins are modified so the chromatin is condensed (heterochromatin).
Transcription factors and RNA polymerase cannot bind to the ERV gene.
No mRNA is transcribed, so the viral envelope proteins are not synthesised.

questions.question: Explain why the viral envelope proteins expressed in cancer cells could be used in a vaccine against cancer cells, using the information in the question.
questions.answer: The envelope proteins are expressed in the cancer cell membrane but not in normal cells, so they act as specific antigens; a vaccine stimulates immune cells to destroy cancer cells displaying them.
steps: In cancer cells the viral envelope proteins are synthesised and incorporated into the membrane.
Normal cells do not express these proteins, so they are specific to cancer cells.
A vaccine containing these proteins as antigens stimulates B cells and T cells to respond.
Memory cells and T killer cells are produced that recognise the protein on cancer cells and destroy them.

questions.question: Calculate how many tonnes of rice are lost if 20% of the harvest (1.7 million tonnes per year) is lost, in standard form.

questions.question: Explain why it is important to identify rice plants infected with RYMV as early as possible.
questions.answer: Early identification allows infected plants to be removed or treated before the virus spreads to other plants, reducing crop loss.
steps: The virus spreads from infected plants to healthy plants, often by insect vectors.
Early identification lets farmers remove or isolate infected plants before the virus spreads.
This limits the proportion of the harvest lost and protects the yield.
Early action limits the spread of the virus and the yield loss.

questions.question: Suggest why wavelengths of light between 400 nm and 900 nm were used in this investigation.
questions.answer: This range covers visible light and near-infrared, which are strongly absorbed or reflected by leaf pigments and structure, so differences can be detected.
steps: 400 to 900 nm covers visible light (400 to 700 nm) and some near-infrared.
Plant pigments such as chlorophyll absorb strongly in the visible range, so changes show up here.
Near-infrared is strongly reflected by healthy leaf structure, so changes are also detected.
Visible and near-infrared wavelengths are reflected by leaf pigments and structure.

questions.question: Explain why the scientists thought there would be a difference in the reflection spectra for healthy and RYMV-infected leaves.
questions.answer: Infection causes yellow or orange streaks, which means less chlorophyll, so the leaves absorb and reflect light differently.
steps: RYMV infection causes discolouration with yellow or orange streaks on the leaves.
This indicates reduced chlorophyll and changed pigment content in the leaf cells.
Pigments absorb light at specific wavelengths, so less absorption and more reflection occur at those wavelengths.
So the reflection spectra of infected and healthy leaves differ.

questions.question: Explain why rice plants from Africa are less susceptible to RYMV than those imported from Asia.
questions.answer: African rice has been exposed to RYMV for a long time, so natural selection favoured resistant varieties; Asian rice has not been exposed and lacks these alleles.
steps: Rice in Africa has been exposed to RYMV over many generations.
Random variation produced some plants with resistance alleles (for example, altered virus-binding proteins).
Plants with resistance survived and reproduced, so the resistance alleles became more common (natural selection).
Asian rice had no exposure to the virus, so it had no selection for resistance and is more susceptible.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term pathogen.
questions.answer: An organism, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist, that causes disease.
steps: A pathogen is a disease-causing microorganism.
Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protoctists.
They cause disease by damaging cells or producing toxins.
Pathogens can be bacteria, viruses, fungi or protoctists.

questions.question: State the meaning of the term antibiotic.
questions.answer: A substance produced by microorganisms (or synthetic) that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria.
steps: Antibiotics are substances produced by microorganisms such as fungi or bacteria, or synthetic versions.
They kill bacteria or inhibit their growth.
They do not act on viruses.
Antibiotics do not act on viruses.

questions.question: Explain how treatment with antibiotics can affect the gut flora.
questions.answer: Antibiotics kill susceptible gut bacteria, reducing diversity and changing proportions, which allows resistant or harmful species to increase.
steps: Antibiotics kill or inhibit sensitive bacteria in the gut flora.
This reduces the variety and changes the proportions of the bacterial species present.
Resistant bacteria are not killed, so they increase in proportion (no competition).
The balance of gut flora is disrupted, which can reduce protection against pathogens.

questions.question: Which types of immunity result in the production of antibodies (options A to D)?
questions.answer: A: artificial active and natural active.
steps: Antibodies are made by the body's own B cells in active immunity (natural or artificial).
Artificial active immunity comes from vaccination; natural active from infection.
Passive immunity (artificial or natural) involves antibodies received from elsewhere, not made by the person, so B and D are wrong.
Option A is correct because both forms of active immunity produce antibodies.

questions.question: Explain why a single antibody had to be made by the scientists, using the diagrams of antigens and two antibodies.
questions.answer: The cancer cell and the T killer cell have different antigens, so one antibody with two binding sites is needed to link them together.
steps: A cancer cell has an antigen that a T killer cell cannot bind directly.
A T killer cell has its own antigen, which a cancer-specific antibody does not bind.
A single antibody with two binding sites can bind the cancer antigen and the T killer cell antigen at the same time.
This brings the T killer cell and cancer cell together, so the T killer cell can destroy the cancer cell.

questions.answer: The antibody binds the cancer cell and a T killer cell at once, bringing them together so the T killer cell destroys the cancer cell.
steps: The antibody binds an antigen on the cancer cell with one binding site.
Its other binding site attaches to the T killer cell.
This holds the T killer cell next to the cancer cell.
The T killer cell then releases perforin or triggers apoptosis, destroying the cancer cell.

questions.question: Describe how to inoculate the liquid broth using colonies growing on nutrient agar.
questions.answer: Use a sterile inoculating loop to pick a colony from the agar, then transfer it into the sterile broth under aseptic conditions near a flame.

Pick a single colony from the nutrient agar plate using the loop.

Close the broth container and the agar plate immediately, working near a Bunsen flame.

questions.question: Suggest why these liquid cultures were shaken in an incubator.
questions.answer: Shaking supplies oxygen to the aerobic bacteria and mixes the culture so cells and nutrients are evenly distributed.
steps: Shaking increases the dissolved oxygen in the broth, which aerobic bacteria need for respiration.
It keeps the cells suspended and evenly distributed in the medium.
Mixing also keeps the temperature and nutrients uniform, so growth is consistent.
Shaking therefore improves growth of the culture.
